deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Discretionary Relocation

For dental practitioners, a lease is more than a real estate agreement; it is a blueprint for clinical operations. A standard relocation clause, often buried in the miscellaneous sections of a commercial lease, grants landlords the unilateral right to move your practice to another unit within the complex. While seemingly benign, these clauses are frequently drafted with extreme ambiguity regarding what constitutes a 'comparable' space.

The primary danger lies in the landlord's ability to redefine 'comparable' based on square footage alone, ignoring the specialized infrastructure required for dental success. A move to a space with insufficient plumbing, inadequate electrical capacity for imaging equipment, or poor street visibility can effectively destroy a practice's patient retention and revenue streams.

Identifying the Infrastructure Trap

Landlords exploit vague language to avoid the high costs of dental-grade build-outs. Without specific protections, you may find yourself responsible for:

  • Upgrading plumbing lines to support dental chairs and suction systems.
  • Reconfiguring electrical panels to accommodate high-voltage medical equipment.
  • Absorbing the costs of new signage and ADA-compliant accessibility modifications.
  • Managing the significant downtime and loss of patient revenue during the transition.

Establishing Market-Standard Protections

An elite-level lease negotiation must move beyond simple 'comparability' and demand 'functional equivalence.' To protect your practice, your relocation clause must include the following non-negotiable pillars:

  • Technical Specification: The new space must meet all existing clinical, plumbing, and electrical specifications without additional tenant expense.
  • Full Cost Indemnification: The landlord must bear 100% of the costs for construction, permits, architectural fees, and even the cost of updating your professional signage.
  • Business Interruption Compensation: If the relocation requires a period of clinical downtime, the landlord should provide a rent abatement period or direct compensation for lost revenue.
  • Right of Refusal: The tenant must have the right to reject any space that fails to meet the pre-defined technical criteria.

title: Standard Market Terms in Relocation Clauses for Dental Offices
